From the above ingredients reiterated by this Court, It is clear that an unlawful demand for dowry is not a pre requisite element to constitute "cruelty" under Section 498A IPC.

It suffices that the conduct falls within either of the two broad categories outlined in clauses (a) or (b) of the provision, namely, wilful conduct likely to cause grave injury or mental harm (clause a), or harassment intended to coerce the woman or her family to meet any unlawful demand (clause b).
Therefore, either form of cruelty, independent of a dowry demand, is sufficient to attract the provisions of Section 498A IPC and make the offence punishable under the law.....
16.

Before this Court, the Respondents have contended that the wilful conduct described in clause (a) of the Explanation to Section 498A IPC should only be treated as cruelty if it is accompanied by a dowry CA No.111/2024 Alka Vs. State PS Lajpat Nagar Page No.16 of 33 demand as outlined in clause (b), or that an unlawful demand for property or valuable security, standing alone, constitutes cruelty under Section 498A.

17. Therefore, upon careful examination of the relevant provisions of Section 498A IPC, the precedents cited, and the factual matrix of the case, it is apparent that the High Court's decision to quash the criminal proceedings against Accused Nos.1 and 2 was flawed.

Section 498A IPC recognizes two distinct forms of cruelty: one involving physical or mental harm in clause (a) and the other involving harassment linked to unlawful demands for property or valuable security in clause (b).
These two provisions are to be read disjunctively, meaning that the presence of a dowry demand is not a prerequisite for establishing cruelty under the Section.
The allegations made by the Appellant, which detail instances of physical abuse and harassment, fall within the scope of "cruelty" as defined under clause (a) of Section 498A IPC.
The absence of an explicit dowry demand does not negate the applicability of the provision where acts of physical violence and mental distress have been demonstrated.

It further explains "cruelty" means:
"(a) any wilful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman; or (b) harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand".
29. Concept of cruelty U/s 498A IPC need not be physical. Even mental torture or abnormal behaviour may amount to cruelty or harassment in a given case.

Mental cruelty varies from person to person depending upon the intensity and the degree of endurance, some may meet with courage and some others suffer in silence, to some it may be unbearable and a weak person may think of ending once life.

The object of adding the aforesaid offence was to punish husband and his relatives who torture and harass the CA No.111/2024 Alka Vs. State PS Lajpat Nagar Page No.28 of 33 wife Alka Sharma vs State on 9 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/88830926/

sentences.text: with a view to coerce her or any person related to her to meet unlawful demands or to drive her to commit suicide.

To constitute an offence u/s 498A IPC, it is required that a woman must be married, she must be subjected to cruelty or harassment and such cruelty or harassment must have been shown either by husband of the woman or by the relative of the husband.
Any kind of assault upon a woman, offends her dignity.
Therefore, the prosecution needs to prove at the first place that there was an "unlawful demand" and secondly, that the harassment caused to her on account of her failure to meet the unlawful demand.
It is not every type of harassment or cruelty that would attract an offence U/s 498A IPC, and therefore, the expression cruelty as defined under the Section has to be taken into consideration.
The word willful contemplates obstinate and deliberate behaviour on the part of the accused for it shall amount to cruelty.
Thus mens rea, is an essential ingredient of the offence.
Therefore, a bare vague and general statement that the behaviour of the accused persons was bad towards the complainant cannot be said prima facie to constitute an offence U/s 498A IPC.

Further the offence contemplate the harassment of a woman to coerce her or her relative to meet the unlawful demand for any property or valuable security, and therefore, it is required to prove that such demand was made.

Mere demand of dowry will not attract an offence U/s 498A IPC, and therefore, it is required for complainant to show that the demand was unlawful and the same caused harassment and cruelty to her or mentally tortured her.

A critical provision addressing cruelty within marriages, Section 498A IPC seeks to protect woman from cruelty by the husband and his family.

Section 498A IPC recognizes two distinct forms of cruelty: one involving physical or mental harm in clause (a) and the other involving harassment linked to unlawful demands for property or valuable security in clause (b).
These two provisions are to be read disjunctively, meaning that the presence of a dowry demand is not a prerequisite for establishing cruelty under the Section.
The allegations made by the Appellant, which detail instances of physical abuse and harassment, fall within the scope of "cruelty" as defined under clause (a) of Section 498A IPC.
The absence of an explicit dowry demand does not negate the applicability of the provision where acts of physical violence and mental distress have been demonstrated.

This Court has repeatedly laid down that the mere fact that a view other than the one taken by the trial Court can be legitimately arrived at by the appellate Court on reappraisal of the evidence cannot constitute a valid and sufficient ground to interfere with an order of acquittal unless it comes to the conclusion that the entire approach of the trial Court in dealing with the evidence was patently illegal or the conclusions arrived at by it were wholly untenable.
While sitting in judgment over an acquittal the appellant Court is first required to seek an answer to the question whether the findings of the trial Court are palpably wrong, manifestly erroneous or demonstrably unsustainable.
If the appellant Court answers the above question in the negative the order of acquittal is not to be disturbed.
Conversely, if the appellant Court holds, for reasons to be recorded, that the order of acquittal cannot at all be sustained in view of any of the above infirmities it can then - and then only - reappraise the evidence to arrive at its own conclusions.

To constitute an offence u/s 498A IPC, it is required that a woman must be married, she must be subjected to cruelty or harassment and such cruelty or harassment must have been shown either by husband of the woman or by the relative of the husband.
Any kind of assault upon a woman, offends her dignity.
Therefore, the prosecution needs to prove at the first place that there was an "unlawful demand" and secondly, that the harassment caused to her on account of her failure to meet the unlawful demand.
It is not every type of harassment or cruelty that would attract an offence U/s 498A IPC, and therefore, the expression cruelty as defined under the Section has to be taken into consideration.
The word willful contemplates obstinate and deliberate behaviour on the part of the accused for it shall amount to cruelty.
Thus mens rea, is an essential ingredient of the offence.
Therefore, a bare vague and general statement that the behaviour of the accused persons was bad towards the complainant cannot be said prima facie to constitute an offence U/s 498A IPC.
Further the offence contemplate the harassment of a woman to coerce her or her relative to meet the unlawful demand for any property or valuable security, and therefore, it is required to prove that such demand was made.
Mere demand of dowry will not attract an offence U/s 498A IPC, and therefore, it is required for complainant to show that the demand was unlawful and the same caused harassment and cruelty to her or mentally tortured her.

Further in the present matter, the complainant has alleged that she was treated with cruelty by the accused persons from the date of her marriage in February, 2005 till she stayed with the accused persons on 26.11.2008 but all the allegations levelled against accused persons are vague, omnibus and not supported by any documentary evidence.
Further, there is no iota of evidence against the accused persons to hold them guilty for the offence U/s 498A IPC as there is no specific material on record and there are no specific allegations against any of the accused persons in the CA No.111/2024 Alka Vs. State PS Lajpat Nagar Page No.31 of 33 complaint filed by the complainant or in the testimony recorded before the Ld. Trial Court.
Mere general allegations of harassment without pointing out specific incidents against the accused persons would not be sufficient to convict the accused for the offence charged.
The allegations of the complainant are vague, and unsupported by any concrete evidence or medical records.
The allegations against the accused persons are not specific regarding time, place or events that could legally established cruelty U/s 498A IPC.
Mere omnibus allegations against the accused persons without substantiation, cannot justify the allegations to be proved.
34. In the present matter the complainant has levelled general and vague allegation and has failed to mention or show as to which accused had committed what offence and what was the role played by the accused persons in the commission of the offence.
Under such circumstances, it would be an abuse of process of law to convict the accused persons as the complainant has failed to specify the allegations of cruelty towards the accused persons.
Therefore, in the present facts and circumstances, the allegations against the accused persons for committing offence U/s 498A IPC does not stand proved and the Ld. Trial Court has rightly acquitted them for the offence U/s 498A/34 IPC.

State PS Lajpat Nagar Page No.32 of 33 examined by the prosecution, there is no corroboration in the testimonies of witnesses and the case of the prosecution have not been proved beyond reasonable doubts.
